summary: Gives implementation guidelines for using return codes in MGCP version 1.0 as defined in RFC 3435. Because the return codes cannot cover every situation, the document focuses on helping a Call Agent that receives a code to behave appropriately and consistently. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a gadget answers with a number, the sender must know what that number means. This guide helps phone systems react to those answer numbers the same sensible way every time.

questions: how should a call agent handle mgcp errors
mgcp temporary failure vs service failure
subtitle: How MGCP gateways should pick return codes, and how Call Agents should react to them, grouped into behavior categories.

tldr.problem: The return codes in MGCP 1.0 (RFC 3435) cannot cover every situation a gateway may meet, so different Call Agents could react to the same code in different ways.
tldr.mechanism: The document sorts return codes into categories based on the behavior expected of the Call Agent, then walks through each code with its valid commands, typical situation and category.
tldr.outcome: Gateways get guidance on choosing a code when no specific one fits, and Call Agents get consistent handling for each category. The document updates RFC 3435.

sections.title: Why Categorize Return Codes
sections.content:
This document gives implementation guidelines for return codes in the Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) version 1.0, defined in RFC 3435. The return codes there cannot cover every specific situation a gateway may meet, and the document says that is neither possible nor necessary. What matters is that the Call Agent that receives a code behaves appropriately and consistently.

The solution is to categorize the return codes gateways send, based on the behavior expected of the Call Agent. Gateway developers can use the categories to choose a suitable code when no specific one exists, and Call Agent developers can use them to act consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone system cannot have a special number for every possible problem. So the numbers are put in groups, and each group says what the phone system should do next.

sections.title: The Return Code Categories
sections.content:
Seven kinds of grouping are defined. Codes in normal are part of ordinary operation and are not errors. Codes in none belong to specific situations that trigger a specific Call Agent behavior, so they share no common category.

  • Service Failure: the endpoint is out of service, or the Call Agent should treat it as if it were.
  • Provisioning Mismatch: the gateway says it does not support what the Call Agent asked, possibly because their provisioning is out of step. Such errors should be weeded out during integration testing.
  • Temporary Failure: the current call is likely permanently affected, but later calls on the same endpoint may succeed once resources free up. The change is not expected within tens of milliseconds, but may come within seconds or minutes.
  • State Mismatch: the Call Agent and gateway disagree on state, and the Call Agent can fix it by making a more suitable request.
  • Remote Connection Descriptor Error: a mismatch between the two gateways in the call. Per RFC 2327, unrecognized SDP attributes should be ignored and should not cause an error.

Exact Call Agent behavior may depend on endpoint type, whether it is the originating or terminating side, and call state. The document only recommends that behavior be consistent for a given combination of call state and category.
sections.plainLanguage: Problems are sorted into boxes such as "this line is broken", "try again in a bit", "you asked for something I can't do" and "we disagree about what's happening". Each box has its own way to react.

sections.title: Codes, Situations and Categories
sections.content:
Section 2.2 describes each code with the commands it is valid for, the situation that triggers it and its category. A response valid for a NotificationRequest (RQNT) is also valid for a connection command carrying an encapsulated RQNT, and the same holds for EndpointConfiguration.

The 000 to 250 codes are normal. 000 is a response acknowledgement, 100 says a transaction is in progress (a provisional response for something slower than the normal retry timer, such as a CreateConnection using RSVP), and 101 says it was queued. When a queue reaches its high-water mark, the entity starts sending 101 until the queue drops to the low-water mark, and the Call Agent should throttle back its request rate. 200 and 250 report success, the latter for a DeleteConnection.

The 4xx codes are mostly transient. 400 is an unspecified transient error and should be avoided if a more specific code exists. 401 and 402 mean the phone is already off-hook or on-hook (State Mismatch). 403 means temporary lack of gateway resources, 404 means insufficient bandwidth, and 409 means internal overload, after which the Call Agent SHOULD throttle back.

The 5xx codes are mostly permanent. 500 means the endpoint is completely unknown, and 501 that it is out of service. 502 is permanent lack of resources, 504 an unknown command, and 518 an unsupported or unknown package. 505 to 509 and 527 relate to the Remote Connection Descriptor, and 515, 516 and 540 are state mismatches. The last code described is 541, for an invalid or unsupported Local Connection Option.
sections.plainLanguage: Every number has a short story about when to use it. Numbers starting with 1 and 2 mean "all is fine", those starting with 4 mean "try again", and those starting with 5 mean "this won't work as asked".

sections.title: Choosing Between Similar Codes
sections.content:
Several codes sit close together, and the document says which to prefer. Use 403 for temporary resource shortage, and 502 only when future requests are expected to fail, for which 529 (hardware error) may be more specific. Use 404 for a bandwidth check that may later succeed, while 526 is for cases where the same codec will keep failing.

Likewise, 405 is the normal code for an endpoint that is restarting, and 520 is kept only for backward compatibility with earlier MGCP releases. For events and signals, 522 means the name is not in the package, 512 or 513 mean the package is only partly implemented, and 518 means the package itself is unknown. Some categories can shift by circumstance: a 404 may prompt trying a lower bandwidth codec, and a 503 may be recovered by sending separate requests without the wildcard.

Where the RFC marks a code with an asterisk in its summary table, the Call Agent may treat it as a different category depending on the situation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some numbers sound alike, so the guide says which to pick. One means "busy right now", while a similar one means "this will never work", and you must not mix them up.

sections.title: Guidelines for Gateways and Call Agents
sections.content:
For gateways, the document recommends mapping situations accurately to codes in the "none" and State Mismatch groups, and using a code from the correct category for the other groups. Gateways should also add commentary with the return code, since MGCP allows it and it helps debugging.

It recommends that 502, 520 and 526 not be used unless the situation is really permanent, since 403, 405 and 404 are almost always more appropriate. A gateway that upgrades from the first set to the second should not reuse the old codes for something else right away, so a Call Agent never has to treat one code in two ways.

For Call Agents, an unrecognized or unexpected code should be handled by its first digit, as outlined in RFC 3435. Within the Service Failure, Provisioning Mismatch, Temporary Failure and Remote Connection Descriptor Error categories, codes should be treated alike. Because RFC 2705 gave little guidance on 502, 520 and 526, Call Agents may have to treat them as 403, 405 and 404 for gateways that have not been updated.
sections.plainLanguage: The gadget should pick the right number and write a note about what went wrong. The phone system should treat numbers in the same group the same way, and if it sees an unknown number it looks at the first digit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document says it merely provides a convenient way to categorize MGCP return codes to help decisions about failure conditions, and that it does not affect MGCP security in any way.
sections.plainLanguage: This guide only sorts the answer numbers into groups, so it does not change how safe the system is.
